Sellout
SEL-owt
noun (Boomer slang)
From the verb sell out: to dispose of all one’s stock (17th century), and in American political slang of the nineteenth century, to betray a cause or party for gain. The noun sellout for such a betrayal, and for the betrayer, became a favorite insult of the 1960s counterculture, hurled at musicians who signed with big labels, activists who took establishment jobs, and anyone who traded ideals for money or comfort. A sellout is also, separately, an event with every ticket sold.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A sellout is a person who abandons his principles for money, fame, or comfort — the folk singer who goes commercial, the radical who joins the corporation. In 1968 it was the worst thing one hippie could call another. The Christian observation: the insult names a real sin, and Scripture records its two great examples. Esau "for one morsel of meat sold his birthright" (Heb 12:16), trading what was eternal for what was immediate. And Judas went to the chief priests and "said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver" (Mat 26:15). Our Lord put the whole matter in one question: "For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" (Mar 8:36). Paul named the root: "the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows" (1Ti 6:10). But the counterculture’s use of the word had a blind spot. It called a young man a sellout for taking a job, marrying, and supporting a family — that is, for growing up. Scripture calls that faithfulness. The real sellout is not the man who works for a living but the man who sells the truth. A father can teach his son the difference: never sell your soul, your conscience, or your Lord; and never be ashamed of honest work.

Webster 1828 Definition

Boomer counterculture insult for one who betrays principles for money or comfort — the sin of Esau (Heb 12:16) and Judas (Mat 26:15), though the hippie wrongly applied it to honest work and family duty.

SELLOUT, n. (Boomer slang, 1960s–present; from 19th-c. political sell out) 1. A person who betrays principles, a cause, or a community for personal gain. 2. The act of such a betrayal. 3. (unrelated) An event for which all tickets are sold. v. to sell out.

Webster (1828) — SELL, verb transitive preterit tense and participle passive sold . [ 1. To transfer property or the exclusive right of possession to another for an equivalent in money. It is correlative to buy , as one party buys what the other sells . It is distinguished from exchange or barter , in which one commodity is given for another; wheras in selling the consideration is money, or its representative in current notes. To this distinction there may be certain exceptions. ’Esau sold his birthright to Jacob for a mess of pottage.’ But this is unusual. ’Let us sell Joseph to the Ishmaelites- And they sold him for twenty pieces of silver.’ Genesis 37:27 . Among the Hebrews, parents had power to sell their children. 2. To betray; to deliver or surrender for money or reward; as, to sell one’s country. 3. To yield or give for a certain consideration. the troops fought like lions, and sold their lives dearly.

Decode for families: ask what a person is being accused of selling. If it is his conscience, the charge is grave. If it is his time for a paycheck, it is not a charge at all.

Modern Corruption

The counterculture rightly despised betrayal for gain but wrongly called ordinary responsibility a sellout; Scripture condemns selling the soul and honors honest work.

expand to see more

Every generation has its sellouts, and the Boomer generation coined the word for them with real moral passion. It was right to despise the artist who wrote what sold rather than what was true, and the activist who abandoned the poor for a comfortable office. That is Esau’s profanity and Judas’s silver. But the word was used too widely. It became a weapon against anyone who chose stability over rebellion, and it taught a generation to despise the ordinary virtues — showing up, paying bills, raising children — that hold a society together. Paul’s counsel to work with one’s own hands is not selling out; it is the gospel lived on a Tuesday.

The irony of the word is that many who used it most loudly in 1968 sold out most completely later — not by getting jobs but by abandoning every conviction they had once held, including the true ones. The only way not to sell out is to belong to Someone who cannot be bought. The believer has been bought already, "not with corruptible things, as silver and gold," but with the precious blood of Christ.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English sellan (to give, to hand over) → sell out (17th c., dispose of all; 19th-c. US political, betray) → 1960s counterculture noun sellout.

Old English sellan — to give, to hand over, to deliver up

17th c.: sell out — to dispose of all one’s goods or shares

19th-c. American political slang: sell out — to betray a party or cause for gain

1960s counterculture: sellout — one who abandons ideals for money or comfort

Scripture: Esau (Gen 25:33; Heb 12:16); Judas (Mat 26:15)
